title: Bellarmine: venials are beside the law—imperfect will or imperfect lex
source_text: XXVII. Bellarminus vero contendit recte dici peccata venialia, cujuscunque tandem generis sint, non esse contra legem, sed praeter legem: quia si sunt contra praeceptum aliquod legis proprie dictae, ut peccata venialia, quae dicuntur ex subreptione, quale est desiderium rei illicitæ non plane deliberatum, non sunt perfecte voluntaria: adeoque hoc ipso non sunt perfecte contra legem, nisi materialiter, quia lex proprie voluntati tantum nostrae ponitur. Vel si perfecte voluntaria sunt, praeceptum quod transgrediuntur non est perfecte & in rigore lex. Nam, inquit, cum finis praecepti sit charitas, & ex fine mensurentur praecepta, si quod praeceptum constituatur de re, quae parum admodum ad eum finem pertineat, ut si speciali praecepto caveatur, ne quis verbum otiosum loquatur; id praeceptum non poterit esse perfecte & in rigore, & ut alii ajunt, antonomastice lex. De Amiss. Grat. & statu Pecc. lib. 1. cap. 11. sub finem.
pass_a_gloss: But Bellarmine contends that it is rightly said that venial sins, of whatever kind they finally are, are not against the law but beside the law: because if they are against some precept of law properly so called, as venial sins which are said from surprise—such as a desire of an illicit thing not fully deliberate—they are not perfectly voluntary: and so by that very fact they are not perfectly against the law except materially, because law is properly laid upon our will alone. Or if they are perfectly voluntary, the precept they transgress is not perfectly and in rigor a law. For, he says, since the end of a precept is charity, and precepts are measured from the end, if some precept is established about a matter which pertains very little to that end—as if by a special precept it is forbidden that anyone speak an idle word—that precept will not be able to be perfectly and in rigor, and as others say, antonomastically, a law. On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, book 1, chapter 11, toward the end.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine: surprise-venials lack perfect voluntariness, so they are not perfectly against law except materially.
Fully willed minor precepts (idle words) are not ‘law’ in rigor, since charity barely measures them.

choices.why: Law in the emphatic proper sense.
